subject: Re: Pegasus AI - dedicated GPU SKU tradeoffs and sizing
messages:
From: Samira Khan <samira@pegasus.ai>

Cc: Carlos Mendes <carlos.m@pegasus.ai>

Subject: Dedicated GPU options inquiry

Hi Markus,

Quick background: Pegasus runs a mixed product. Two primary workloads: (1) real-time chat assistants (low latency, 95ms target p50, 300ms p99), median user prompt ~60 tokens, responses ~120 tokens, peak concurrent users ~450 (expected to double in 6mo); (2) large-batch embedding/semantic search jobs (offline, high throughput, average request is ~1k tokens, sometimes large batches up to 50k tokens total per job).

We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated and want guidance on SKU selection & sizing: H100 vs A100 (40/80) vs L4. Key questions:
- Which SKUs fit our real-time chat latency SLO while keeping unit cost reasonable?
- For embedding/batch throughput, where does A100 vs H100 make sense?
- Are there workable hybrid mixes (percentages) to cover both cost and performance?
- Memory-sensitive case: some customers send long context windows (~100k tokens) for summarization — when do we need H100?

I can share a representative query profile and token distributions if that helps. Would like a concise recommendation and an initial sizing estimate so procurement can start POC budget.

Thanks,
Samira
COO, Pegasus AI

Hi Samira — thanks, this is a great summary. Short answer up front: a hybrid approach is almost always the best starting point.
High-level guidance:
- L4: lowest cost per token for short-context, low-memory chat where models are quantized and batch sizes are moderate. Good for p50 latency but less headroom on p99 under bursty concurrent short requests.
- A100 (40GB / 80GB): the balanced workhorse. A100 80GB is a solid choice for medium-long context workloads and batch embedding throughput — better memory for KV cache and fewer sharding constraints.
- H100 (80GB+ variants): necessary primarily when you need 1) maximum memory headroom for very large contexts or multi-model ensembles on a single host, or 2) the best fp16/fp8 perf on specific kernels under high-throughput inference patterns.

I attached a draft cost model (sku-cost-model.xlsx) with ballpark relative unit costs and a simple throughput table. To give a rough starting point based on your numbers:
- For chat (median 60/120 tokens, target p99 300ms): target a primary pool of A100 for steady traffic with an autoscaled L4 pool for cost-efficient short requests and bursts.
- For embeddings (large batches): treat as batch workers on A100 80GB; burst H100 if latency-sensitive heavy jobs appear.

Looping in Monica (capacity forecasting) and Aditya (solutions) — Monica, can we get a fleet mix + week-one pilot plan if Pegasus provides the detailed query profile? Aditya, will you own the pilot run and test vectors?

- Markus

Markus Klein

Samira / team — I pulled together a quick synthesis after looking at the initial profile you sent (attached as pegasus-query-profile.csv). Key observations and recommendation in bullets:

- Traffic mix: ~72% short conversational requests (<200 tokens), ~20% medium batch/embeddings, ~8% long summarization jobs (>10k tokens occasionally).
- Latency SLO: 300ms p99 for chat implies we need low-queuing headroom; A100-backed pools with continuous batching tuned to small max batch windows provide predictable latency.
Recommendation (pilot configuration):
- Core pool (A100 80GB) — 6 instances: handle steady chat + medium batches; optimistic baseline throughput per A100 (chat-equivalent) = ~300 concurrent short requests with proper batching and KV cache.
- Cost pool (L4) — 8 instances: route lightweight short-context traffic here; use cost-rules (e.g., requests <150 tokens, no KV cache hit) to keep unit costs down.
- Burst / large-context pool (H100) — 2 instances: reserved for long-context summarization and large ensemble requests; used rarely but necessary to avoid sharding complexity.
- Autoscaling & fallbacks: prefer routing policy that tries L4 first for qualifying requests, then A100; H100 only for requests flagged as long-context or labeled "need_h100".

Sizing notes / sample calc:
- Estimated peak concurrent short-context requests = 900 -> distribute across L4 + A100 such that p99 remains under 300ms.
- Embedding batch throughput target: target 4–6 large batches/hour; A100 80GB gives better amortized GPU-hours for these jobs.

I attached the sample profile and included a short config-snippet.txt with routing snippets for Redwood Dedicated. Happy to run a pilot with these counts for 7 days to collect real telemetry.

—Monica

Thanks Monica — this is helpful. A couple follow-ups:

1) Memory-bound embeddings: we have an internal customer that wants 8k-d embeddings (float16) and they sometimes send very large documents that expand to ~40GB of raw activation memory per model instance. Is A100 40/80 enough or do we need H100 to avoid model sharding across nodes? What are the operational tradeoffs if we shard?

2) Quantization: do you have safe recommendations for 4-bit or 8-bit quant that Redwood supports in Dedicated? If aggressive quant reduces memory enough, we could avoid H100 in many cases.

3) Fallback / SLA behavior: if H100s are busy, can requests be routed to A100 in a degraded mode (e.g., shorter context) automatically? What's the best practice for preserving availability vs quality?

—Carlos
Head of Engineering, Pegasus AI
From: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.ai>
To: Carlos Mendes <carlos.m@pegasus.ai>, Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>, Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.ai>
Date: Sat, 19 Jun 2027 14:15:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Pegasus AI - dedicated GPU SKU tradeoffs and sizing

Carlos — quick answers from the infra side:

1) Memory-bound embeddings and sharding: A100 80GB will handle many large models but if a single request requires >80GB of activation/KV state, you either shard (model parallel / tensor-slicing) or move to H100 with larger effective memory and better multi-instance perf. Sharding increases network overhead and can add 10–30% latency depending on topology. If your workload needs single-host processing for consistent latency, H100 is the safer choice.

2) Quantization: Redwood Dedicated supports 8-bit and production-validated 4-bit flows for many open architectures. 4-bit can significantly reduce memory (roughly 2–4x vs fp16 for params); activations remain a factor. For embeddings, quantized models often preserve enough quality, but we recommend running a small eval set (we can do this in pilot) to confirm.

3) Fallbacks and graceful degradation: our routing engine supports policy-based fallbacks. Two patterns we recommend:
  - Quality-first: queue on H100 until capacity available (risk higher latency).
  - Availability-first: route to A100 with enforced context clipping and a policy tag indicating degraded quality.
We can implement automatic fallback with a custom policy that tries H100, then A100 with context-trim, then returns a 503 if neither are available.

Snippet (config-snippet.txt) outlines a simple routing policy and context-trim hook. We'll also instrument a small QoE metric in the pilot to measure quality delta when falling back.

—Dev

Thanks everyone — summary and next steps:

Summary decisions (pilot):
- Pilot fleet: A100 80GB (6x), L4 (8x), H100 (2x reserved).
- Routing policy: L4 for qualifying short requests -> A100 steady-state -> H100 for flagged long-context. Fallback to A100 with context-trim if H100 unavailable.
- Quantization: test 8-bit and 4-bit in pilot for embedding models; run small eval set to validate quality.

Action items:
- Pegasus: provide final sample dataset + any embargoed long-context examples (Samira).
- Redwood (Aditya/Monica): prepare pilot config and pricing estimate for the 7-day pilot using the attached sku-cost-model.xlsx.
